live.title: A real NiPoPoW proof — GET /nipopow/proof/{{m}}/{{k}}
live.caption: Each orange tick is a header included in the proof. The early chain needs only a few scattered superblocks; towards the tip the sampling gets denser, and the last {{k}} blocks are included in full. Data from node <node>{{node}}</node>.

intro: To check for yourself that a transaction is in the Ergo chain, the “proper” way is to download every block header — over 1.8 million of them, ~220 bytes each — and verify each one's proof-of-work. For a phone, or for a smart contract on another blockchain, that is far too much. NiPoPoWs (Non-Interactive Proofs of Proof-of-Work) shrink that header chain down to a few hundred headers while keeping equivalent confidence.

superblock.title: Superblocks: some blocks are “luckier” than others
superblock.p1: A miner has to find a PoW solution below the target T (see Difficulty & nBits). But solutions are often much smaller than required: on average one block in 2 has a solution below T/2, one in 4 is below T/4, and one in 2μ is below T/2μ. Such a block is called a level-μ superblock.
superblock.level1: Level 1: about half of all blocks.
superblock.levelMu: Level μ: about 1/2<sup>μ</sup> of all blocks — the highest level in a chain of n blocks is roughly log<sub>2</sub>(n).
superblock.p2: The key idea: a level-μ superblock “contains” an expected 2μ ordinary blocks' worth of work. So instead of presenting the whole chain, a prover can present just the chain of superblocks at a high level — far fewer blocks, representing an equivalent amount of proof-of-work. Nobody can fake superblocks: producing a level-20 block requires being a million times luckier than for an ordinary block.
superblock.figAlt: A chain of 24 blocks drawn as a skip list. Every block is level 0; every 2nd block also reaches level 1, every 4th level 2 and every 8th level 3. Orange interlink arrows jump back from block 24 to 16 to 8 along level 3, and blocks 21 to 24 are marked as the last k blocks. An arrow points to a NiPoPoW proof of just four headers, next to a much taller stack labelled full chain.
superblock.figCaption: Superblocks form a ladder: the higher the level, the rarer the block. A proof climbs the high levels through the interlinks (only the top level's are drawn), steps down to lower levels near the tip and adds the last k blocks in full — so a few hundred headers can stand in for almost two million. (Idealised: real superblocks land at random, not at exact multiples.)

interlink.title: Interlinks: back-pointers to every level
interlink.p1: A normal header has a single back-pointer: parentId. To jump from one superblock to the previous one at the same level without walking every block in between, each Ergo block also carries an interlink vector: after the genesis id in the first slot, there is one entry per level: the id of the most recent superblock of that level before it. The vector lives in the block's extension section (the header commits to it through extensionHash), together with a Merkle proof so anyone can verify it without the whole extension. Today the vector has about 21 entries: the genesis id plus about 20 levels, roughly log₂ of a ~1.9-million-block chain.
interlink.noteTitle: Why Ergo has had it since block 1
interlink.note: Bitcoin could add interlinks with a “velvet fork” (miners add extra data; old nodes ignore it), but hasn't. Ergo was designed by researchers closely connected to the NiPoPoW work, so interlinks have been in every block since genesis — no fork required.

proof.title: What is in a proof?
proof.p1: A NiPoPoW proof has two security parameters and three parts:
proof.m: The minimum number of superblocks required at each level used — larger means harder to cheat, and a longer proof.
proof.k: How many blocks at the tip are always included in full (like a “confirmation count”), because the tail is not yet settled.
proof.prefix: The superblock chain from genesis to near the tip, taken at the highest level that still has m blocks, then descending to lower levels near the tip.
proof.suffix: The last k headers, with the interlinks of the first of them to connect to the prefix.
proof.p2: The proof at the top of this page uses m = {{m}}, k = {{k}}. An Ergo node serves it through the API /nipopow/proof/{m}/{k} — and you can ask for a proof up to a specific block with /nipopow/proof/{m}/{k}/{headerId}.

verify.title: Whom does the verifier trust?
verify.p1: The verifier doesn't need to trust any node. It asks several nodes for proofs and keeps the best one. To compare two proofs:
verify.step1: Find the last block both proofs have in common — everything before it is agreed on.
verify.step2: After that point, score each proof on its own: for every level μ where it still has at least m blocks, compute 2<sup>μ</sup> × (number of level-μ blocks). The proof's score is the best of these.
verify.step3: A level-μ block stands for 2<sup>μ</sup> ordinary blocks of work, so the higher score represents more proof-of-work — and wins. The two proofs may be scored at different levels.
verify.p2: As long as at least one of the nodes asked is honest, the result is correct — the same “honest majority of hash power” assumption the blockchain itself rests on.
verify.warn: A NiPoPoW proves “this chain has the most proof-of-work”, not that every transaction is valid — that still takes a full node. An application that accepts a single proof (say, a contract on another chain) must set a minimum-work threshold and wait for enough confirmations.

spv.title: Compared with Bitcoin SPV (Electrum)
spv.p1: Bitcoin light wallets such as Electrum use the SPV model (Simplified Payment Verification) Satoshi described in the whitepaper: download every block header (80 bytes each), verify the proof-of-work of the whole chain, then ask Electrum servers for a Merkle proof of each transaction you care about. NiPoPoWs keep that idea but replace “every header” with “a few hundred superblocks”:

headers.label: Headers to download
headers.btc: All of them — roughly 950 thousand headers × 80 bytes ≈ 75 MB (2026), growing linearly forever
headers.ergo: A few hundred at most — the proof at the top of this page has ~30 KB of headers (well under 200 KB with the interlinks and their Merkle proofs), growing with the log of the chain length

inclusion.label: Proving a transaction is in the chain
inclusion.btc: Merkle branch to the block header
inclusion.ergo: Merkle branch to the header, plus a NiPoPoW proof that the header is on the heaviest chain

balance.label: Checking a balance / UTXOs
balance.btc: You must trust the server: it can hide some of your transactions
balance.ergo: Verifiable yourself with an AVL+ proof against the header's stateRoot — the server cannot hide anything

trust.label: Trust model
trust.btc: Honest majority of hashrate; server honest about address history
trust.ergo: Honest majority of hashrate; at least one honest node among those asked

contract.label: Verification inside a contract on another chain
contract.btc: Practically impossible — 75 MB of headers won't fit in a contract
contract.ergo: Feasible — tens of KB, enough for sidechains and bridges

phone.label: On a phone
phone.btc: Electrum ships hard-coded “checkpoints” to skip old headers — i.e. you trust the developers
phone.ergo: No checkpoints needed: the proof stands on its own from genesis

spv.p2: Neither model checks that individual transactions are valid — that is still a full node's job. The difference is that NiPoPoWs make “verify the chain” cheap enough for even a smart contract to do, and Ergo's stateRoot closes the biggest hole in SPV: the server cannot lie about the UTXO set. Bitcoin could get NiPoPoWs through a velvet fork, but hasn't deployed them so far.

uses.title: What does Ergo use NiPoPoWs for?
uses.bootstrap: Fast node bootstrapping: an Ergo node can start from a NiPoPoW proof (requested from several peers, keeping the best one) and then download a UTXO-set snapshot, instead of syncing from block 1. Enable it with ergo.node.nipopow.nipopowBootstrap = true. The Ergo docs estimate a proof for several years of chain at only 30–40 KB, versus a UTXO snapshot of a few hundred MB.
uses.light: Light clients: a phone wallet verifies the chain with a few hundred headers instead of nearly two million, combined with the stateRoot to verify boxes.
uses.mining: Logarithmic-space mining: miners keep only the important superblocks instead of the whole history.
uses.bridges: Sidechains and bridges: a contract on another chain can verify that “event X happened on Ergo” from a proof — the basis for two-way pegs and cross-chain atomic swaps without a trusted intermediary.
uses.p1: Node 6.0.5 tightened three checks: the m/k parameters of a requested proof are validated, each header's proof-of-work is verified before it is used for bootstrapping, and invalid m/k parameters from peers are rejected.
